rubric.why: A supersaturated solution contains more dissolved solute than a saturated solution at the same temperature.
rubric.description: Defines a supersaturated solution by comparison with a saturated solution at the same temperature.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for the complete definition; 1 mark if it says the solution contains extra solute but omits the comparison or temperature.

modelAnswer: A supersaturated solution contains more dissolved solute than a saturated solution can normally hold at the same temperature.

items.followUp: Define a 0.5 M solution and state how you would prepare 1 dm³ of it using NaOH.

rubric.why: Molarity is the number of moles of solute in one dm³ of solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that one mole of solute is present in one dm³ of solution.

rubric.why: The molar mass of NaOH is 40 g mol⁻¹, so 40 g is needed for 1 dm³ of a 1 M solution.
rubric.description: Gives the amount and volume for preparing 1 M NaOH.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for specifying 40 g NaOH and making the solution up to 1 dm³.

modelAnswer: A molar solution contains one mole of solute in one dm³ of solution.
The molar mass of NaOH is 40 g mol⁻¹, so weigh 40 g of NaOH.
Dissolve it in some distilled water, transfer to a 1 dm³ volumetric flask, and add distilled water up to the mark.

items.followUp: What is a dilute solution, and how can a concentrated solution be made dilute?

rubric.why: A concentrated solution has a relatively large amount of solute compared with the solvent.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for indicating that it contains a large amount of solute relative to the solvent.

rubric.why: Adding solvent increases the solution volume without adding solute, so the concentration decreases.
rubric.description: Explains how a concentrated solution is diluted.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that adding solvent lowers the concentration.

modelAnswer: A concentrated solution contains a relatively large amount of solute dissolved in a given amount of solvent.
It is diluted by adding more solvent, which lowers its concentration.

items.followUp: Define reduction in terms of oxygen and give an example.

rubric.why: Oxidation is defined in terms of oxygen as the addition of oxygen to a substance.
rubric.description: Defines oxidation as the addition of oxygen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct definition.

rubric.why: The reaction shows magnesium combining with oxygen to form magnesium oxide.
rubric.description: Gives a correct example of oxidation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid example, such as magnesium forming magnesium oxide.

modelAnswer: Oxidation, in terms of oxygen, is the addition of oxygen to a substance.
For example: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO.

items.followUp: Write two chemical properties of metals.

rubric.why: Non-metals generally form acidic oxides when they react with oxygen.
rubric.description: States that non-metals form acidic oxides with oxygen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this property, with a correct example if given.

rubric.why: Non-metals react with metals to form ionic compounds.
rubric.description: States that non-metals react with metals to form ionic compounds.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this property, with a correct example if given.

modelAnswer: Non-metals react with oxygen to form acidic oxides; for example, C + O₂ → CO₂.
Non-metals react with metals to form ionic compounds; for example, 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl.

items.followUp: Write a balanced chemical equation for the reaction of sodium hydroxide with bromine.

rubric.why: Chlorine reacts with sodium hydroxide to form sodium chloride, sodium hypochlorite, and water; the equation must be balanced.
rubric.description: Writes the balanced reaction of chlorine with sodium hydroxide.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for the correct balanced equation; award 1 mark for the correct products or an otherwise correct but unbalanced equation.

modelAnswer: Chlorine reacts with cold, dilute sodium hydroxide as follows:
Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaOCl + H₂O.

items.followUp: Describe Rutherford’s alpha-particle scattering experiment and state the conclusions he drew from it.

rubric.why: The experiment directed alpha particles at thin gold foil and detected their scattering using a fluorescent screen.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for identifying the alpha particles, thin gold foil, and detecting screen; award 1 mark if one essential element is missing.

rubric.why: Most alpha particles passed through the foil without deflection.
rubric.description: States the observation that most particles passed straight through.

rubric.why: Some alpha particles were deflected through small angles.
rubric.description: States that some particles were deflected.

rubric.why: A very small number of alpha particles were turned back or reflected.
rubric.description: States that a very few particles were turned back.

modelAnswer: Rutherford directed a narrow beam of alpha particles from a radioactive source at a very thin gold foil.
A fluorescent zinc sulphide screen around the foil detected the particles by flashes of light.
Most alpha particles passed straight through the foil without deflection.
Some alpha particles were deflected through small angles.
A very few alpha particles were deflected backwards.

items.followUp: Write four differences between a mixture and a compound.

rubric.why: The proportions of substances in a mixture can vary.
rubric.description: States that a mixture has variable composition.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying variable composition.

rubric.why: The components of a mixture retain their individual properties.
rubric.description: States that mixture components retain their properties.

rubric.why: Mixture components can be separated by physical methods.
rubric.description: States that mixture components are separable by physical methods.

rubric.why: A mixture does not have a definite melting or boiling point like a pure substance.
rubric.description: States that a mixture has no fixed melting or boiling point.

modelAnswer: A mixture has a variable composition.
The substances in a mixture retain their individual properties.
The components of a mixture can be separated by physical methods.
A mixture does not have a fixed melting point or boiling point.
